title: Orcas Are Bumping Boats — And Scientists Think It's Playtime!
summary: Imagine you're sailing along the coast of Spain. Suddenly, a giant black fin pops out of the water. Then — BONK! — something whacks the bottom of your boat. That's what's been happening to sailors off Spain and Portugal since 2020. A small group of fewer than 50 orcas (also called killer whales) keeps ramming boats. On July 23, 2026, a group of orcas hit a sailboat called Idem again and again. They smashed the rudder — the part that steers the boat — until water rushed in and the boat sank. Luckily, the two people on board were rescued. Three other boats met orcas that same day. One lost its steering and had to be towed to port. On August 29, four orcas broke half the rudder off a 42-foot yacht. The five people on board still made it back safely. Two days later, another yacht needed a rescue ship to guide it into port in Baiona, Spain. So why are the whales doing this? Scientists first wondered if the orcas wanted revenge. They quickly said no. Now many experts think the whales are just playing. The tuna they eat have become easier to find, so young orcas have extra free time. One scientist, Bruno Díaz López, thinks the boats are like practice targets for hunting. "This is like a training toy," he said. One sad thing: in September, someone shot Toñi, the oldest orca in the group, with a pellet gun. She's healing now. Scientists say boaters should stay away from orca areas and make loud banging noises to keep the whales away.
why_it_matters: It shows that when people and wild animals share the same waters, we have to figure out how to live safely together — for the animals and for us.

background_read: Orcas, or killer whales, are actually the biggest kind of dolphin, and they live in oceans all over the world.
The boats in this story sail near the Strait of Gibraltar (a narrow stretch of sea between Spain and Morocco), where Atlantic bluefin tuna swim past every year.
Scientists have been studying these orca encounters since 2020, and they say the whales are not usually trying to hurt people.
Article_Structure: WHO: A group of fewer than 50 orcas off Spain and Portugal, plus the sailors on boats like the Idem and a 42-foot yacht
WHAT: The orcas keep ramming boats and breaking rudders — one sailboat sank, and other boats needed towing or a rescue ship
WHERE: The coasts of Spain and Portugal, including the port of Baiona, Spain
WHY: Many experts think the young orcas are simply playing and practicing hunting, because tuna are easier to find and the whales have extra free time

perspectives.description: They say the whales are probably just playing or practicing hunting, not getting revenge, and they want people to understand the orcas aren't being mean on purpose.
For them the danger is real: rudders get smashed, boats sink, and people need rescuing, so they want practical ways to keep their boats and crews safe.

perspectives.perspective: People who care about animal safety
perspectives.description: They point out that the danger goes both ways — someone shot the oldest orca, Toñi, with a pellet gun, so the whales can be hurt too.
